title: Bit energy, symbol energy and noise
heading: A bit-energy value belongs to a declared bit rate
problem: how average signal power is distributed among information bits, coded bits and symbols.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="energy-per-bit-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="energy-per-bit-title">Bit energy, symbol energy and noise</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="55" y="110" width="190" height="90" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="148.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Information</text><text x="150.0" y="173.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">4 Mbit/s</text><rect x="280" y="110" width="190" height="90" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="375.0" y="148.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">Coded bits</text><text x="375.0" y="173.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">8 Mbit/s</text><rect x="505" y="110" width="190" height="90" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#7651a7" stroke-width="2"/><text x="600.0" y="148.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#7651a7">QPSK symbols</text><text x="600.0" y="173.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#7651a7">4 Msym/s</text><text x="450" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">One watt of average received signal power</text><text x="150" y="260" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#176a70">Eb,info = 0.25 µJ</text><text x="380" y="260" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#ad5f13">Eb,coded = 0.125 µJ</text><text x="630" y="260" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#7651a7">Es = 0.25 µJ</text><text x="450" y="335" text-anchor="middle" font-size="21" fill="#17343d">A rate-1/2 code; two coded bits per QPSK symbol</text><text x="450" y="385" text-anchor="middle" font-size="21" fill="#17343d">Energy = average power ÷ the matching event rate</text></g></svg>
explanation: An energy axis is useful only with its counting convention. Information bits describe the useful encoder input. Coded bits include redundancy. A modulation symbol labels m = log₂M coded bits. With code rate r = Rinfo/Rcoded, the rates satisfy Rcoded = Rinfo/r and Rs = Rinfo/(r m).

For average received carrier power C in watts, Eb, info = C/Rinfo, Eb, coded = C/Rcoded and Es = C/Rs, all in joules. Therefore Eb, coded = r Eb, info and Es = r m Eb, info. Changing r at fixed C and Rinfo preserves energy per information bit while changing the other energies and downstream rates.

Use N₀ as one-sided noise power density in W/Hz; a real noise process has two-sided density N₀/2. With equivalent noise bandwidth BN in hertz, N = N₀BN. Then Eb/N₀ = (C/N)BN/Rb and Es/N₀ = (C/N)BN/Rs. The bit rate Rb must match the chosen Eb. A full occupied RF width and a receiver equivalent noise bandwidth need not be numerically equal.

The adjustable figure holds received power and information rate fixed, varies coding and symbol labels, and separately computes in-band C/N using a declared noise bandwidth. Framing and pilots are excluded. A BER curve must use the same energy convention as the link calculation.
example: At C = 1 W, Rinfo = 4 Mbit/s, rate 1/2 and QPSK, Rcoded = 8 Mbit/s and Rs = 4 Msym/s. Eb, info = Es = 0.25 µJ, while Eb, coded = 0.125 µJ. If BN = 2 MHz, Rinfo = 4 Mbit/s and C/N = 10 dB, Eb, info/N₀ = 10 × 2/4 = 5, or 6.99 dB.

questions.prompt: At fixed received power and information rate, how do the two bit energies change when code rate drops from 1 to 1/2?
questions.hint: Apply C/R separately at the encoder input and output.
questions.answer: Information-bit energy stays unchanged. Coded rate doubles, so coded-bit energy halves. Bandwidth or symbol loading must accommodate that greater coded rate.

questions.prompt: When does a quoted C/N equal Eb/N₀ numerically?
questions.hint: Keep the factor BN/Rb.
questions.answer: When the noise bandwidth BN equals the bit rate Rb under the declared conventions. The general relationship retains BN/Rb; equal units alone do not establish equality.

title: BPSK decisions and Gaussian error tails
heading: A noisy sample becomes a decision at a threshold
problem: how a synchronized binary receiver counts the chance that noise crosses its decision threshold.
explanation: A coherent receiver aligns the carrier phase and samples the matched-filter output. In the simple BPSK model the transmitted coordinate is +A or −A, and the observation is y = s + n. Noise n is Gaussian with mean zero and standard deviation σ in the same amplitude units. Equal prior probabilities and equal error costs place the optimum threshold at zero.

Both error events matter: Pb = p₊P(y < τ | +A) + p₋P(y > τ | −A). At equal priors and τ = 0, symmetry reduces this to Q(A/σ). The Q function is the standard Gaussian upper-tail probability: Q(x) = ∫ₓ∞ exp(−u²/2)du/√(2π) = ½erfc(x/√2). BER is dimensionless; multiplying by bit rate gives an expected error count per second.

In a unit-energy signal basis, A = √Eb and σ² = N₀/2, giving coherent uncoded BPSK Pb = Q(√(2 Eb/N₀)). Convert a dB energy ratio to linear form before taking the square root. This model assumes perfect synchronization, Gaussian noise and no residual intersymbol interference.

The adjustable threshold shows why a biased threshold trades one conditional error against the other. With bit-one prior p₊, equal costs and common variance, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) threshold is τ = σ² ln((1−p₊)/p₊)/(2 A). The figure keeps the selected threshold separate from that optimum; unequal priors change which mistakes are more frequent.
example: At Eb/N₀ = 0 dB, the linear ratio is 1 and Pb = Q(√2) = 0.07865. At 10 dB, Pb = Q(√20) ≈ 3.87×10⁻⁶. For equally likely bits, vanishing signal amplitude approaches Pb = ½.

questions.prompt: Why do both transmitted symbols contribute the same conditional error probability at a zero threshold?
questions.hint: Reflect the Gaussian density around zero.
questions.answer: The +A and −A densities are mirror images with the same variance. Their tails beyond the opposite side of zero have equal area; the equal prior weights then sum to one.

questions.prompt: If ones become more frequent, which direction should the equal-cost threshold move?
questions.hint: A more frequent +A symbol needs less observation evidence to select it.
questions.answer: It moves negative. With p₊>½, ln((1−p₊)/p₊) is negative, making +A the decision over a larger observation region.

explanation: An M-point alphabet carries m = log₂M coded bits per symbol. A symbol error occurs whenever the receiver selects the wrong point. Its bit cost depends on the transmitted and selected labels. Gray labeling makes neighboring labels differ by one bit, helping when nearest-neighbor errors dominate. In Fig. 1, read the horizontal I pair first and the vertical Q pair second. Dashed lines are decision boundaries halfway between adjacent coordinates.

For coherent square M-QAM, equally likely symbols, perfect timing and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), put q = Q(√(3 Es/((M−1)N₀))) and a = 1−1/√M. The in-phase and quadrature coordinates are independent. Each coordinate is correct with probability 1−2 aq, so exact SER is Ps = 1−(1−2 aq)² = 4 aq−4 a²q².

At sufficiently high SNR with Gray labels, Pb ≈ 4 aq/log₂M. This approximation omits the squared-tail term and assumes mainly one wrong bit per nearest-neighbor error. The lecture’s compact 4 aQ expression is a nearest-neighbor SER approximation; treating it as an exact BER would confuse the two event counts.

For Gray QPSK, Es = 2 Eb and Pb = Q(√(Es/N₀)) = Q(√(2 Eb/N₀)), the same ideal BER as BPSK at equal energy per bit. Equal energy per symbol instead gives QPSK half as much energy per bit. The plotted QAM formula applies to square grids; APSK rings require their own detection model.
example: For square 16-QAM at Es/N₀ = 10 (10 dB), q = Q(√2) ≈0.07865 and a =0.75. Exact SER is about 0.2220, while the high-SNR Gray-BER approximation is about 0.05899. At this modest SNR, the approximation assumptions deserve attention.

questions.prompt: Can a measured 10% symbol-error fraction alone determine the bit-error fraction of 16-QAM?
questions.hint: Count bits changed by each incorrect decision.
questions.answer: Additional labeling and error-transition information is needed. Each wrong symbol can change different numbers of its four bits.

questions.prompt: Why do BPSK and Gray QPSK agree on an Eb/N₀ plot but differ on an Es/N₀ plot?
questions.hint: QPSK divides a symbol’s energy between two orthogonal bit coordinates.
questions.answer: Uncoded QPSK has two bits per symbol, so Es =2 Eb. Equal bit energy yields the same coordinate detection problem; equal symbol energy gives each QPSK bit half as much energy.

title: Satellite PSK and APSK constellations
heading: Ring geometry combines phase choices with a few amplitude levels
problem: how the DVB-S2 constellation families trade symbol loading against noise separation and amplifier constraints.
explanation: The satellite lecture uses QPSK, 8PSK, 16APSK and 32APSK as a sequence of larger alphabets. They map two, three, four and five coded bits per symbol. At equal symbol rate, a larger alphabet increases coded throughput; at equal average energy, packing more alternatives generally demands a cleaner received signal.

PSK places every symbol on one radius. APSK uses several radii and several phases: 16APSK contains 4 inner and 12 outer points; 32APSK contains 4+12+16. The figure normalizes the mean squared point radius to 1 for equally likely symbols. Its ring-radius ratios are explicitly illustrative, not a chosen standard MODCOD.

A satellite high-power amplifier can compress large envelope values to improve power efficiency. Ring structure limits amplitude levels to a few groups but does not eliminate nonlinear distortion. AM/AM changes amplitude; AM/PM changes phase. The existing amplifier-and-backoff topic explores a declared limiter model rather than predicting a real hardware BER.

Equal symbol-center radii do not establish constant envelope between symbols after pulse shaping. A receiver still needs carrier and timing synchronization, distortion estimation and appropriate decision boundaries. Satellite rain fading can favor a smaller constellation or a lower coding rate as link margin falls.
example: At 5 Msym/s, 8PSK maps 15 Mbit/s of coded labels and 32APSK maps 25 Mbit/s. With an effective rate 3/4 and no further overhead, those correspond to 11.25 and 18.75 Mbit/s of information. These arithmetic rates supply no BER guarantee.

questions.prompt: How many points belong to the outermost ring of the 32APSK family illustrated here?
questions.hint: Keep the total 32 and the inner 4+12.
questions.answer: Sixteen points lie on the outermost ring. The full ring populations are 4+12+16.

questions.prompt: Why can a one-ring PSK constellation still show peaks after filtering?
questions.hint: Follow the continuous transition between two symbol-center points.
questions.answer: Pulse shaping superposes time-shifted pulses during transitions. The continuous envelope can vary even though the allowed symbol-center coordinates share one radius.

title: DVB-S2: from payload to waveform
heading: A broadcast profile joins coding, mapping, framing and pulse shaping
problem: how a useful bit stream passes through the protection and waveform stages of a satellite broadcast.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="dvbs2-chain-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="dvbs2-chain-title">DVB-S2: from payload to waveform</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="200" y="35" width="500" height="52" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="67.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Information + BB header</text><line x1="450" y1="87" x2="450" y2="110" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="200" y="110" width="500" height="52" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="142.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">BCH outer code</text><line x1="450" y1="162" x2="450" y2="185" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="200" y="185" width="500" height="52" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="217.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">LDPC inner code</text><line x1="450" y1="237" x2="450" y2="260" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="200" y="260" width="500" height="52" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#7651a7" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="292.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#7651a7">Bit mapping and physical framing</text><line x1="450" y1="312" x2="450" y2="335" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="200" y="335" width="500" height="52" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="367.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Pulse shaping and RF transmission</text><text x="450" y="440" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#17343d">At reception: synchronize → demap → decode.</text></g></svg>
explanation: DVB-S2 supplies selectable satellite modulation-and-coding profiles. In the transmit chain, an outer BCH block code adds protection, an inner LDPC code adds further constraints, a mapper assigns coded bits to symbols, and physical framing supplies synchronization and optional pilots. A receiver reverses these roles after synchronizing. Bit interleaving is used for 8PSK and APSK; the QPSK path bypasses that interleaver.

For occupied raised-cosine RF width B and rolloff α, the channel sends Rs = B/(1+α) symbols per second. Each mapped data symbol carries m = log₂M coded bits. The rate during mapped symbols is mRs. Across a complete physical frame, only a fraction ηPL of the symbols carry these bits, giving a frame-average coded bit rate of ηPL mRs. Coding and the baseband header further reduce the useful payload rate.

A normal FEC frame contains 64,800 LDPC-coded bits, or 64,800/m mapped symbols. Each physical frame adds a 90-symbol header. When enabled, 36-symbol pilot blocks follow every 16 slots of 90 mapped symbols, except at the frame boundary. If the transmitted frame lasts T seconds, the frame-average coded bit rate is 64,800/T. The filled-frame payload rate is (KBCH − 80)/T, where KBCH is the BCH input length and 80 bits carry the baseband header.

Each profile pairs a supported inner code rate with a constellation. The figure assumes a full baseband frame and excludes input-packet and padding losses. The lecture’s inner-LDPC rates span 1/4 through 9/10. At the QPSK end, lowering rate can provide more protection while reducing useful throughput. These controls account for resource usage. Link feasibility also needs a profile’s required received quality and a selected error target.
example: For a 6 MHz channel, QPSK at α = 0.35 carries 8.89 Mbit/s during mapped symbols. At α = 0.20, 32APSK carries 25 Mbit/s during mapped symbols, a ratio of 2.8125. With the figure’s QPSK 3/4 profile, α = 0.25 and pilots on, the same channel sends 4.8 Msym/s. Its 33,282-symbol frame lasts 6.934 ms. The 64,800 coded bits average 9.346 Mbit/s, and the 48,328 payload bits average 6.970 Mbit/s.

questions.prompt: Why does selecting a listed inner rate 3/4 fail to establish that 75% of every RF symbol is useful payload?
questions.hint: Follow both coding stages and the framing resources.
questions.answer: BCH parity, the baseband header, the physical header and any pilots also use resources. The useful fraction needs the complete chain, not only the inner-LDPC ratio.

questions.prompt: If a fade already forced QPSK, how can the system trade still more throughput for protection?
questions.hint: A MODCOD contains a coding choice as well as a constellation.
questions.answer: It can choose a supported lower coding rate. More of the transmitted stream then carries redundancy, reducing useful information rate while potentially improving reliability for the stated decoder.

title: Product parity and a correctable error
heading: A failed row and failed column locate one changed bit
problem: how row and column parity turn a small data block into a single-error-correcting code.

stroke-width="2"/><text x="502.5" y="298.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">1</text><text x="450" y="405" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">Four information bits → nine transmitted bits; rate 4/9.</text></g></svg>
explanation: An even-parity check requires the XOR of its complete group to be 0. XOR is addition modulo 2: 1⊕1 = 0. Adding one parity bit detects every odd number of flips in that group, but two flips can cancel. A failed single check indicates inconsistency without locating the changed position.

The figure arranges four information bits as a 2×2 block and appends row and column parity, including a corner check. The result has nine coded bits, so code rate r = 4/9. Every row and column has even parity. With exactly one error anywhere in the 3×3 block, one failed row and one failed column intersect at the changed bit.

The adjustable model selects up to two distinct bit positions to flip. A displayed repair is justified only when the selected channel model contains exactly one error. For multiple errors, check patterns alone may be ambiguous. Four changes at a rectangle’s corners can preserve every parity check and escape detection.

This tiny product code illustrates the purpose of structured redundancy. A practical LDPC decoder has many coupled sparse constraints and soft reliability; its graph, block length and error performance require their own model. The nine-bit demonstration is not the DVB-S2 code.
example: Data [[1, 0],[1, 1]] become [[1, 0, 1],[1, 1, 0],[0, 1, 1]]. Flip the left bit of the middle row: only that row and the first column fail. Their intersection identifies the flipped bit. The five added bits are code overhead, not additional user data.

questions.prompt: If a parity-bit location rather than a data-bit location flips once, does the row/column method still locate it?
questions.hint: Check every row and every column, including the parity row and column.
questions.answer: Yes. A single flip anywhere belongs to one row and one column, so their failed checks still intersect at that position.

questions.prompt: Why can four flips at a rectangle’s corners pass every check?
questions.hint: Count changed bits separately within each touched row and column.
questions.answer: Each affected row and column contains two flips, an even number. Their XOR checks therefore keep the original parity even though the data differ.

title: Block codes and Hamming distance
heading: The decoder compares a received word with a structured codebook
problem: how modulo-two encoding creates legal codewords and distance determines a correction guarantee.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="block-code-distance-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="block-code-distance-title">Block codes and Hamming distance</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="70" y="80" width="200" height="80" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Data 101</text><line x1="270" y1="120" x2="340" y2="120" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="340" y="80" width="220" height="80" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="113.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">Multiply by G</text><text x="450.0" y="138.5" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">modulo 2</text><line x1="560" y1="120" x2="630" y2="120" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="630" y="80" width="200" height="80" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="730.0" y="126.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Codeword 101010</text><text x="450" y="245" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">Received 101011 differs from 101010 in one position.</text><text x="450" y="310" text-anchor="middle" font-size="21" fill="#17343d">Search 8 legal codewords within 64 possible received words.</text><text x="450" y="380" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">Nearest Hamming distance: count differing bits.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A binary block code maps k information bits to n coded bits, with r = k/n. For a row-vector convention, c = dG mod 2, where d is 1×k, G is k×n and c is 1×n. A column convention uses the transpose. Matrix dimensions and the multiplication order belong together.

The lecture’s teaching example has G rows 100101, 010011 and 001111. Its identity block makes it systematic: the first three output bits reproduce the data. For d = 101, XOR the first and third rows to obtain c = 101010. The model enumerates all eight valid codewords and compares the selected received word using Hamming distance.

The minimum distance between distinct valid words is dmin = 3. Membership checking can detect up to dmin−1 changes, while unique nearest-word decoding can correct up to floor((dmin−1)/2) arbitrary changes. Those are different guarantees. A received word with too many errors can be closer to the wrong valid word.

Nearest Hamming decoding corresponds to equally likely codewords and independent symmetric bit flips with crossover probability below ½. A soft decoder uses the reliability of observations as well. The selected error mask is a reproducible example, not a statistical channel or a guaranteed-recovery claim beyond one arbitrary flipped bit.
example: For transmitted 101010 and received 101011, the unique nearest valid codeword is 101010 at distance 1. This code corrects that example and every other single-bit error; some two-bit errors are miscorrected. Repeating two copies of a bit only detects disagreement, while three copies support a majority decision.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of G when a row of three information bits produces six coded bits?
questions.hint: Make(1×3)G produce 1×6.
questions.answer: G has shape 3×6. A 6×3 matrix belongs to the corresponding column-vector convention with multiplication Gd.

questions.prompt: Does dmin =3 guarantee that every two-bit error can be corrected?
questions.hint: Compare the detection bound with the correction bound.
questions.answer: It guarantees detection of up to two changed bits when checking valid-word membership, and correction of one arbitrary changed bit. Two-bit nearest-word recovery is not guaranteed.

title: Convolutional coding and memory
heading: Each output pair depends on the current bit and two stored bits
problem: how a rate-one-half encoder turns input history into a constrained output sequence.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="convolutional-code-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="convolutional-code-title">Convolutional coding and memory</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="90" y="90" width="160" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Current input u</text><rect x="370" y="90" width="160" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Delay 1</text><rect x="650" y="90" width="160" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="730.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Delay 2</text><line x1="250" y1="125" x2="370" y2="125" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="530" y1="125" x2="650" y2="125" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450" y="260" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" fill="#176a70">v₁ = uₜ ⊕ uₜ₋₁ ⊕ uₜ₋₂</text><text x="450" y="315" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" fill="#ad5f13">v₂ = uₜ ⊕ uₜ₋₂</text><text x="450" y="405" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">One input bit → two coded bits; K = 3, memory = 2.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A convolutional encoder continuously mixes the current information bit with stored earlier bits. The illustrated tap sets are 111 and 101: v₁, t = uₜ⊕uₜ₋₁⊕uₜ₋₂ and v₂, t = uₜ⊕uₜ₋₂. Each bit clock emits the ordered pair (v₁, v₂).

This binary single-input encoder has nominal code rate 1/2. Constraint length K = 3 counts the current bit plus two stored bits, giving memory 2 and 2² =4 possible memory states. A finite block may append tail bits to end in a known state; termination or puncturing changes its effective rate.

The adjustable figure shows a four-bit input and advances through its four clock steps from initial memory 00. States are shown before and after each input, so current input, delay contents and output timing can be traced separately. The outputs are XOR results, not ordinary sums retained as integers.

A Viterbi decoder compares permitted state paths over many samples and retains survivor paths with the best accumulated metric. A hard-input metric can count bit disagreement; a soft metric uses observation reliability. Larger constraint length grows the state space and decoding cost. The lecture develops the encoding and path idea; a full Viterbi implementation is beyond this figure.
example: From memory 00, input 1010 gives output pairs 11|10|00|10. For the second input 0, the stored history is 10: the upper XOR gives 1 and the lower XOR gives 0. Input ordering and output-pair ordering must remain explicit.

questions.prompt: Why does K =3 correspond to four memory states rather than eight here?
questions.hint: Separate the current input from bits stored between clocks.
questions.answer: Only two bits are stored, so there are 2² =4 memory states. K includes the present input bit in the tapped span.

questions.prompt: At fixed input rate, what happens to transmitted coded-bit rate for this unpunctured encoder?
questions.hint: One information bit generates a pair.
questions.answer: It doubles. Tail bits can add further overhead for finite terminated blocks; a nominal 1/2 rate excludes that boundary cost.

title: Hard decisions and soft reliability
heading: Samples with the same hard bit can carry different evidence
problem: how a log-likelihood ratio keeps information that a hard zero-or-one decision discards.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="soft-decisions-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="soft-decisions-title">Hard decisions and soft reliability</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><line x1="80" y1="225" x2="820" y2="225" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="450" y1="70" x2="450" y2="300" stroke="#506970" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="230" cy="225" r="7" fill="#ad5f13" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#ad5f13">bit 0</text><circle cx="430" cy="225" r="7" fill="#ad5f13" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="400" y="155" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#ad5f13">bit 0</text><circle cx="470" cy="225" r="7" fill="#176a70" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="500" y="155" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#176a70">bit 1</text><circle cx="690" cy="225" r="7" fill="#176a70" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="690" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#176a70">bit 1</text><text x="450" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">A sign labels the bit; distance from zero retains evidence.</text><text x="450" y="355" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" fill="#17343d">L(y) = ln[p(y|1)/p(y|0)] = 2Ay/σ²</text><text x="450" y="415" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#17343d">The sign convention assigns bit 1 to +A.</text><line x1="400" y1="164" x2="430" y2="212" stroke="#506970" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="500" y1="164" x2="470" y2="212" stroke="#506970" stroke-width="1.5"/></g></svg>
explanation: A hard decision keeps a bit label. A soft observation also records how strongly the sample supports that label under the channel model. A small positive sample and a large positive sample both produce bit 1 at a zero threshold, but their error evidence differs.

For Gaussian observations with means ±A, common variance σ² and bit 1 assigned to +A, the natural-log likelihood ratio is L(y) = ln[p(y|1)/p(y|0)] = 2Ay/σ². Positive L favors 1 and negative L favors 0. The ratio is dimensionless; its magnitude depends on the noise scale as well as the observed amplitude.

With prior probability p₁, posterior log odds are Lpost = L(y)+ln(p₁/(1−p₁)). A posterior error probability for the selected bit is 1/(1+exp(|Lpost|)) under this model. The adjustable figure separates channel evidence from prior evidence so the effect of each remains visible.

Soft code decoders combine these observations with code constraints. Some software uses the reverse likelihood ratio and sign convention, which must be translated explicitly. Confidence computed under an incorrect channel model can be misleading; the number is not an unconditional physical guarantee.
example: At A = 1, σ = 0.5 and y = 0.1, L = 0.8. With equal priors, the posterior chance of bit 1 is about 0.690. At y = 1.2 with the same noise, L = 9.6 and that probability is about 0.99993. Both samples yield the same hard bit.

questions.prompt: If σ doubles while A and y stay fixed, how does the channel LLR change?
questions.hint: Its denominator is the noise variance.
questions.answer: It falls to one quarter becauseσ² grows by four. The same observation is weaker evidence under a noisier model.

questions.prompt: Does an LLR of 0 mean a measured zero voltage in every receiver?
questions.hint: Separate the likelihood ratio from prior odds and the chosen signal model.
questions.answer: Here channel LLR 0 occurs at y 0, but posterior log odds can be nonzero because of unequal priors. A different observation model or sign convention also changes how sample values map to evidence.

title: Turbo coding and iterative decoding
heading: Two related orderings let constituent decoders exchange new evidence
problem: how interleaving and repeated soft decoding can recover structure missed by isolated decisions.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="iterative-decoding-title" viewBox="0 0 900 460"><title id="iterative-decoding-title">Turbo coding and iterative decoding</title><rect width="900" height="460" fill="white"/><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="50" y="90" width="190" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#176a70" stroke-width="2"/><text x="145.0" y="131.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#176a70">Input u</text><rect x="350" y="40" width="210" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="455.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">Encoder 1</text><rect x="350" y="180" width="210" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#7651a7" stroke-width="2"/><text x="455.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#7651a7">Interleaver</text><rect x="650" y="180" width="210" height="70" rx="5" fill="white" stroke="#ad5f13" stroke-width="2"/><text x="755.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" fill="#ad5f13">Encoder 2</text><line x1="240" y1="125" x2="300" y2="125" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="125" x2="300" y2="75" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="75" x2="350" y2="75" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="125" x2="300" y2="215" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="215" x2="350" y2="215" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="560" y1="215" x2="650" y2="215" stroke="#17343d" stroke-width="2"/><text x="450" y="315" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="#17343d">Transmit u, parity 1 and parity 2 → nominal rate 1/3.</text><text x="450" y="375" text-anchor="middle" font-size="21" fill="#17343d">Soft decoder 1 ⇄ interleave/deinterleave ⇄ soft decoder 2</text><text x="450" y="430" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#17343d">Exchange new reliability; retain the channel evidence.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A parallel-concatenated turbo encoder supplies the systematic data and parity from two constituent encoders. The first sees the original input order; the second sees a known interleaved order. Transmitting one systematic bit and two parity bits per input gives nominal rate 1/3 before boundary overhead.

Interleaving rearranges positions without adding bits. It changes the context of troublesome local patterns. The receiver applies the matching permutation and inverse permutation when exchanging evidence. Puncturing omits specified coded positions to raise code rate; the receiver knows that omission pattern.

Turbo decoding uses soft-input/soft-output constituent decoders. Each combines channel evidence, code constraints and information from the other decoder, then passes the newly obtained contribution, called extrinsic information. Feeding the same evidence back as though it were new would overstate confidence. A loop of ordinary hard-output Viterbi decisions does not supply this probability exchange.

Iterations trade computation, energy and latency for better estimates; they do not guarantee correction of every error. A quoted performance curve needs the code, rate, channel, decoder, iteration limit and error-counting location. The lecture also discusses iterative demapping and decoding, where uncertain symbol labels can be revisited. The figure shows the architecture rather than simulating an unverified BER gain.
example: If an unpunctured encoder transmits 300 coded bits for 100 information bits, its nominal rate is 1/3. Omitting 100 specified parity bits leaves 200 transmitted bits and rate 1/2, before termination or other framing costs. The surviving parity still constrains the same information sequence.

questions.prompt: Which part of the turbo architecture adds redundancy: the interleaver or the parity encoders?
questions.hint: A permutation preserves the length of its input.
questions.answer: The parity encoders add the redundant constraints. The interleaver changes ordering and relationships but does not itself add bits.

questions.prompt: Why exchange extrinsic evidence rather than repeatedly recycle the entire posterior as new evidence?
questions.hint: Track which observations were already used.
questions.answer: Reusing the same channel or prior evidence as though independent would double-count it and can create unjustified confidence. The exchanged contribution should represent the other decoder’s newly inferred information.

heading: Edges state which bits participate in each parity equation
problem: how a parity-check matrix and its graph express allowed codewords and inconsistent observations.

explanation: A binary parity-check matrix H assigns one XOR equation to each row. For a column codeword c, the legal-word condition is Hc = 0 mod 2. A graph draws bit variables as circles and check equations as squares, with an edge exactly where the corresponding H entry is 1.

The six-bit teaching graph uses checks c₁⊕c₃⊕c₄ =0, c₂⊕c₃⊕c₅ =0 and c₁⊕c₂⊕c₃⊕c₆ =0. These checks match the earlier block code. The syndrome H r records failed checks for a received column r. A zero syndrome establishes membership in this code, not that the transmitted information was necessarily recovered.

LDPC means low-density parity-check. Practical long-block LDPC codes have a sparse H and iterative decoders that exchange soft messages among connected variables and checks. Sparsity refers to H; the generator matrix need not be sparse. The tiny graph explains this notation and does not represent a real DVB-S2 block or error-performance prediction.

The adjustable figure uses a six-bit mask: each 1 flips the corresponding transmitted bit. The highlighted checks show the resulting syndrome. The full codebook permits an independent nearest-Hamming comparison. Several bit patterns can share a syndrome; correcting beyond the code’s stated distance guarantee can select a wrong legal word. BCH and LDPC are distinct stages in the DVB-S2 protection chain.
example: For legal word 101010, all three checks are 0. Flipping its sixth bit gives 101011 and syndrome 001: only the third check fails. In this distance-three teaching code, the syndrome identifies that single flipped position, but a different multi-bit pattern can produce the same syndrome. Flipping positions 1 and 4 produces the same syndrome 001: the failed checks alone give no guarantee once two bits can change.

questions.prompt: Why can a zero syndrome fail to prove that no channel error occurred?
questions.hint: Compare the received word with every possible legal transmitted word.
questions.answer: An error can change one valid codeword into another. The received word then satisfies every parity constraint while representing different information.

questions.prompt: Must a generator matrix G be sparse for a code to be called LDPC?
questions.hint: The family’s name identifies its sparse matrix.
questions.answer: The defining sparsity is in the parity-check matrix H. A valid generator can be much denser; it serves a different mapping role.
